Create an effective event response
You should anticipate operational events, both planned (for example,
    sales promotions, deployments, and failure tests) and unplanned (for
    example, surges in utilization and component failures). Use your
    existing runbooks and playbooks to deliver consistent results when
    you respond to alerts. Specify ownership of defined alerts to a role
    or team that is accountable for the response and escalations.
    Understand the business impact of your system components, and use
    this to target efforts when needed. These practices support evidence
    collection, which becomes crucial when performing post-incident
    analysis (also known as root cause analysis (RCA)) after events, and
    then to help prevent recurrence of failures or to document
    workarounds.
AWS helps simplify your event response by providing tools that
    support all aspects of your workload and operations as code. These
    tools help you script responses to operations events and start their
    initiation in response to monitoring data.
With AWS, you can improve recovery time by replacing failed
    components with known good versions, rather than trying to repair
    them. You can then carry out a separate analysis on the failed
    resources.

OPS06-BP03 Define escalation paths
Capability intent
Every alert maps to a documented and ideally automated
          response, with a clear owner and escalation path.
Alert noise is controlled by grouping related signals and
          tuning thresholds against historical data, so operators trust
          the alarms they receive.
Frequent, well-understood events with a safe remediation are
          handled automatically, freeing operators for problems that
          need human judgment.
Escalation paths are pre-agreed: who acts at each tier, the
          permissions they need, and which high-impact actions are
          pre-approved.
Response paths are rehearsed through drills and refined after
          incidents, so they hold up under real conditions.
Common issues to watch for
Alerts fire without a defined response or owner, so a signal
          arrives but nobody knows what to do with it.
Alarm noise trains operators to ignore alerts, so the one that
          matters is missed.
Frequent, well-understood events are handled manually every
          time, consuming operator attention that novel problems need.
Escalation depends on informal knowledge of who to call, so
          the right person is reached late during an incident.
Escalation paths and automated responses are never rehearsed,
          so they fail the first time they are actually used.
